text: Everyone in the town knows which men take the gambling money, and that open knowledge, rather than any mystery, is what the film works on. A lawyer wants to prosecute. His father, an attorney with a longer memory of the place, has no appetite for the fight, and the reluctance is not cowardice: he lives there, and will go on living there after the verdicts. Phil Karlson keeps to a hundred minutes and the tempo of a crime picture, and the National Film Registry has since taken in this small 1955 release about a county's arrangements. Vice, in it, is a business with employees, hours and a payroll. That is what makes prosecution hard. To break the racket is to break neighbours, and the men doing the breaking have to walk the same three streets afterwards.

A colonel commands a regiment on the Northwest Frontier, and the newest lieutenant under him is his own son. That arrangement is the film's real front. Hollywood in 1935 could still stage British India as horses, dress uniform and open country, and Henry Hathaway takes the pageantry seriously enough to make the discipline beneath it feel binding: Colonel Stone is hard on his officers because a frontier post permits nothing else, and hardest on the boy who carries his name. Two career subalterns flank the newcomer, one surly and one blue-blooded enough to treat danger as a question of manners, while Mohammed Khan waits across a border the regiment patrols without controlling. Among the picture's Academy Awards is one for editing, a workmanlike prize that suits a film whose pleasures are largely those of movement.

Austria's secret service picks an agent for the effect she has on men, then sends her to learn what the Russians know. The spying and the seduction are one job, and the film does not pretend they can be told apart. Ninety-one minutes, 1931 — early enough that the sound film was still deciding how much dialogue it needed. Josef von Sternberg directed; the assignment hands him a heroine whose profession is appearance. The listed genres sit in an unstable order: drama, war, romance. A woman paid to manufacture feeling on schedule is a poor bet to keep her own out of the account. The war functions as authorisation rather than subject, giving the service its reason to spend her and giving her a reason to consent. What the National Board of Review honoured that year was, one suspects, this coolness about a transaction nobody names aloud.

A young man climbs out onto a ledge high above a street and will not come back in. What follows is not a chase but a negotiation, conducted at an awkward distance by a policeman who happens to be there, while below the traffic thickens and the pavement fills with people who came to look. Henry Hathaway allows himself 92 minutes and almost no ground: a window, a stone lip, the room behind it. An Academy Award went to the black-and-white art direction, which here means the building is the adversary — its height, its ordinary masonry, the few inches a man has chosen to stand on. The reasons given for his being up there are domestic and unglamorous: parents who withheld affection, a young woman he doubts he can make happy. Nobody on that ledge is discussing philosophy.

Hospitality is a rule before it is a kindness, and the trouble in this house starts with a guest who cannot be told to leave. He comes up from the South, an old acquaintance of the father, and the family in South-Central Los Angeles makes room because refusing is not done. Charles Burnett keeps the scale domestic: grown sons with grievances of their own, a mother's patience, a bed made up for a man nobody quite remembers agreeing to host. Nothing he does is actionable. That is the difficulty. Across 102 minutes the household's small courtesies set like concrete, and the strain falls on whichever member of it is least prepared to be rude. Sundance gave the film a special jury recognition in 1990. The menace in it stays a matter of manners.

A retreat, a field hospital, a love affair carried on between ambulance runs: the Italian front of the Great War as a Hollywood studio staged it in 1957. The scale is the first thing to reckon with. Charles Vidor spends 152 minutes on an English nurse and an American volunteer, a great deal of room for two people to fill, and the Academy Award the picture collected went to a supporting performance — a fair clue to where its current runs, off to one side of the romance. The scholarship on it argues about remaking and about ideology rather than about love, which is the more useful way in: what happens to Hemingway when a studio gives him two and a half hours. His title is kept intact. The terms of the rest of the bargain are the interesting part.

Six years after the surrender, an American production asked audiences to spend two hours hoping that a German soldier gets away with it. He is a prisoner of war, recruited because the US Army needs to know what is massing on the far bank of the Rhine and has nobody else who can walk into Bavaria and ask. Anatole Litvak splits the risk between two such men: one who will do the dirty work for a price, one worn down enough to be moved by what he sees, which in this trade is the more dangerous flaw. The Gestapo's counter-network is shown as patient and efficient, so the threat is paperwork, an accent, a story that does not check out, rather than gunfire. An Academy Award for editing sits among the honours, and in a picture like this that means the management of dread.

Fyodor Karamazov has money and no intention of parting with it, and every exchange in the house bends around that. Richard Brooks films the Russia of 1870 as a place of debts, betrothals and inheritances — instruments, all of them, which is the right instinct for material that could easily turn into a seminar. Dmitri is the eldest, an officer with a uniform and no funds, engaged to a rich woman and in love with one of his father's mistresses. His brothers include an aesthete, a monk, and a servant who is also a son. Two of them can count. One hundred and forty-five minutes is not much for four brothers and a father, so the weight goes to Dmitri and to the money; an Academy Award for a supporting performance points away from the centre. Old men's appetites, young men's arithmetic.

Ninety minutes hold a birth, a marriage and a death in one New Hampshire town, and none of them arrives as news. The town does the work instead: milk on the step, lessons half learned, a courtship between two people who have known each other all their lives, the whole of it set in the century's first decade. The plainness is manufactured. An Academy Award for black-and-white art direction is the giveaway — a street this unremarkable has to be built, dressed and lit until it stops looking built — and the same restraint is asked of everyone in front of the camera. Sam Wood made it in 1940. What the film withholds is emphasis: no scene announces itself as the one that matters, and an ordinary afternoon gets the attention usually reserved for a wedding.

The promise is always the same: win the money back, and then stop for good. Go-ni attaches himself to an older professional, Pyung Gyung-jang, the way an apprentice attaches himself to a trade — watching hands, learning what a shuffle conceals, taking instruction in a craft whose central skill is making other men feel clever. Choi Dong-hoon takes 139 minutes over that education, and time is what a con needs; the pleasure here is procedural before it is criminal. The film is also funny, which alters the risk rather than reducing it, since a man who can be made to laugh can be made to bet again. The Korean Film Archive keeps it among a hundred national titles. What holds it there is the teaching: nobody in it is born a gambler, and every teacher charges.

Three men beat on an anvil and pass a bottle of beer between blows. It runs a minute, and it is the first instance of an action arranged in front of a camera to be performed rather than simply caught. That distinction can sound academic until the bottle appears. Hammering is work; the beer is business, an invented gesture, timed, put there to fill the frame with something other than labour, and it constitutes the whole of the theatre. William K.L. Dickson shot it in 1893, when a minute was enough to constitute a film. The hammering has a rhythm and the bottle interrupts it. Nobody speaks, nobody looks at the lens. The National Film Registry lists the thing, a peculiar honour for sixty seconds of men pretending to smith.

The story exists to get from one stage to the next, and it does not pretend otherwise. A dancer with ambition and a singer with a career drift together and apart, and their attachment supplies the excuse to travel through several decades of Black American entertainment, which the film presents as a retrospective. The device earns its keep: it lets the picture stop, hand a company of performers a stage each, and start again. Seventy-eight minutes leaves room for little but the numbers — dance, band arrangements, comic turns, songs delivered to an audience inside the film so that each one is an occasion rather than an interlude. The romance is thin and appears to know it. The National Film Registry holds the picture, and the case for it is standing in front of the camera.

A winning lottery ticket goes into a nightclub in somebody's jacket and leaves in a robber's sack. Getting it back requires two men with day jobs to run their own investigation through a world with no interest in helping them, each stop a set piece with its own manners to be learned and got wrong. Sidney Poitier directed, and gave himself 104 minutes of comedy built on a dependable engine: a pair of amateurs out of their depth and too committed to quit. The joke is never that the two are fools. It is that the underworld is a bureaucracy, and working-class patience is precisely the wrong instrument for it. Released in 1974 and now in the National Film Registry, it treats a Black city as a place with institutions, comedians and snobberies of its own.

The real disguise is not the mask, it is the yawning. Don Diego Vega passes his days as a gentleman too weary for horses or heroics, and the act works because the people around him would rather believe a rich man's son is harmless. The other half of the arrangement rides at night. What the 1920 picture understands is how physical the conceit has to be: with no spoken dialogue, the difference between the idler and the swordsman lives in posture, timing and the way a body comes through a door, and much of the 107 minutes is a catalogue of such entrances. The Academy Film Archive preserved it in 2012, so the footwork can still be read. Comedy first, then the blade — and the joke is that both are the same skill, applied with the same wrist.
